title: Evaluation and Benchmarking
objectives: Explain why generative AI needs systematic evaluation.
Describe common metrics: BLEU, ROUGE, exact match and LLM-as-a-judge.
Build a small evaluation set and score model outputs.
Compare two models or prompts on the same set.
Discuss how evaluation results guide improvements.
definition: Evaluation and benchmarking measure generative AI quality systematically. A benchmark is a fixed set of examples with reference answers; the model's outputs are scored against them using metrics such as exact match, BLEU, ROUGE or an LLM judge. Evaluation reveals regressions, compares prompts or models, and guides what to improve next.

theory.heading: Why evaluate generative AI
theory.body: Generative output is probabilistic and hard to judge by eye at scale. Evaluation gives a repeatable score so you can tell whether a change helped or hurt. Without it, you are guessing based on a few examples.

theory.heading: Common metrics
theory.body: Exact match scores whether output equals the reference. BLEU and ROUGE measure word overlap for translation and summarisation. LLM-as-a-judge scores quality on a rubric. Choose the metric that fits the task: exact for labels, ROUGE for summaries, judge for open answers.
points: BLEU/ROUGE: word overlap for translation and summarisation.
LLM judge: quality on a rubric.

theory.heading: Building an evaluation set
theory.body: An evaluation set has inputs and reference answers, separate from training data. It should cover common cases and edge cases. Keep it fixed so you can compare different models or prompts on the same examples.

theory.heading: Comparing models and prompts
theory.body: Run the same evaluation set through two models or two prompts and compare scores. Statistical significance matters: a small difference on a tiny set may be noise. Report scores with the set size so results are interpretable.
points: Same set for both models or prompts.
Note the set size for context.

theory.heading: Using results to improve
theory.body: Evaluation tells you what to fix: low exact match means the format or content is wrong; low judge scores on tone mean the prompt needs adjustment. Iterate: change the prompt or data, re-evaluate, and check that the score goes up without regressions elsewhere.
points: Low scores show where to improve.
Change one thing at a time.

example.title: Comparing two prompt styles for summaries
example.body: An evaluation set has 50 news articles with reference summaries. Prompt A scores ROUGE-1 0.62; Prompt B scores 0.68. Prompt B is better on this set, so it is adopted. A human spot-check confirms the improvement is real, not just word overlap.

code.source:
score_a = evaluate(model_a, eval_set)
score_b = evaluate(model_b, eval_set)
print(f'Prompt A: {score_a:.3f}  Prompt B: {score_b:.3f}')
# Adopt the higher-scoring prompt after spot-checking.

demonstration.description: Score two summaries against a reference using word overlap, showing how the metric reflects similarity.

Reference: 'The cat sat on the mat.'
Summary A: 'A cat is sitting on a mat.' → overlap high.
Summary B: 'The dog ran in the park.' → overlap low.
ROUGE-1 A ≈ 0.83, B ≈ 0.00.

demonstration.output: Higher overlap means a higher score and a better summary.

takeaways: Evaluation makes generative AI quality measurable and repeatable.
Use exact match, BLEU/ROUGE or LLM-as-a-judge depending on the task.
An evaluation set has inputs and references, separate from training data.
Compare models or prompts on the same fixed set.
Use results to target improvements and iterate one change at a time.
Note set size so scores are interpretable.

interview.question: Why evaluate generative AI systematically?
interview.answer: Output is probabilistic, so a repeatable score shows whether a change helped or hurt, instead of guessing from a few examples.
interview.explanation: Evaluation catches regressions and measures progress.

interview.question: What is the difference between BLEU and ROUGE?
interview.answer: BLEU measures precision of word overlap, common for translation. ROUGE measures recall of word overlap, common for summarisation.
interview.explanation: Both score n-gram overlap against a reference.

interview.question: What is LLM-as-a-judge?
interview.answer: Another LLM scores output quality against a rubric such as helpfulness, correctness and tone.
interview.explanation: Use it for open-ended answers without a single reference.

interview.question: Why keep the evaluation set fixed?
interview.answer: so the same examples can be used to compare different models or prompts fairly.
interview.explanation: Changing the set makes scores incomparable.

interview.question: How do evaluation results guide improvement?
interview.answer: Low scores reveal the failure mode; you change one thing (prompt or data), re-evaluate, and confirm the score rises without regressions.
interview.explanation: Iterate one change at a time.

practice.title: Score exact match over an evaluation set
practice.objective: Implement exact-match scoring for a batch of predictions and references, as used in benchmarking.
practice.statement: Read an integer N, then N pairs of lines: a prediction and a reference. Normalise each by stripping whitespace and lowercasing. Count exact matches after normalisation. Print the match count and the fraction correct as a decimal rounded to 2 places, separated by a space.
practice.input_format:
Line 1: N.
Next 2*N lines: prediction and reference alternately.
practice.output_format: Two values: match count and fraction, e.g. '3 0.60'.

example.input:
5
cat
cat
dog
Dog
bird
fish
tree
Tree
car
bike

constraints: Print fraction rounded to exactly 2 decimal places.
practice.starter:
n = int(input())
matches = 0
for _ in range(n):
    pred = input()
    ref = input()
    # TODO: normalise, compare, and print count and fraction
practice.solution:
n = int(input())
matches = 0
for _ in range(n):
    pred = input().strip().lower()
    ref = input().strip().lower()
    if pred == ref:
        matches += 1
print(f'{matches} {matches / n:.2f}')
explanation: Read N, then loop reading prediction-reference pairs.
Normalise each with strip() and lower().
Print the count and matches/n formatted to 2 decimals.

quiz.question: What is an evaluation set?
options: Inputs with reference answers, separate from training
quiz.explanation: An evaluation set pairs inputs with reference answers and is kept separate from training data.

quiz.question: Which metric is common for summarisation?
quiz.explanation: ROUGE measures recall of word overlap and is common for summarisation.

quiz.question: Prompt A scores 0.61 and Prompt B scores 0.63 on a 10-example set. Can you conclude B is better?
options: No, the set is too small to be reliable
quiz.explanation: A 0.02 difference on 10 examples may be noise; use a larger set before concluding.

quiz.question: What does exact match measure?
options: Whether output equals reference after normalisation
quiz.explanation: Exact match checks if the prediction equals the reference, typically after strip and lowercase.

quiz.question: Why note the evaluation set size?
options: So scores are interpretable and reliable
quiz.explanation: Small sets make scores noisy; set size tells you how much to trust them.
